claims.evidence: NHS how-to-lower page: cut down on fatty food especially saturated fat; medicine may be needed if cholesterol has not gone down after diet and lifestyle changes; statins most common.
NHS high cholesterol / BHF: it does not usually cause symptoms; NHS Essex ICB stresses testing even when feeling healthy.
NHS: try to cut down on fatty food, especially saturated fat; can still have unsaturated fat.
BHF cholesterol-lowering foods: oats and barley contain soluble fibre (beta-glucan); beans, peas and lentils are good sources of soluble fibre too. Leeds trust leaflet also names oats and barley.
NHS Health Check page says the check usually includes a cholesterol test and is for adults in England aged 40 to 74. The phrase 'lipid profile' did not appear in any returned text.
claims.newSentence: A blood test measures cholesterol, and an NHS Health Check in England may offer it.

claims.evidence: BHF/NHS: too much of a fatty substance called cholesterol in the blood.
Returned text supports that too much LDL can build up in artery walls and narrow them (BHF/HEART UK). 'The body needs some cholesterol' was not stated in returned text.
claims.newSentence: Too much cholesterol in the blood can build up in the artery walls and make them narrower over time.

claims.evidence: HEART UK/BHF: HDL removes excess cholesterol from vessels and returns it to the liver; LDL can build up in artery walls. BHF notes LDL used to be the main measure of harmful cholesterol but non-HDL is now emphasised, so 'the main type' overstates.
claims.newSentence: HDL is often called good cholesterol because it helps clear excess cholesterol from the blood, while LDL is often called bad cholesterol because it can build up in artery walls.

claims.evidence: HEART UK: high cholesterol has no signs or symptoms and a test is the only way to know; NHS Essex: testing important even if you feel healthy.

Returned text lists an unhealthy diet high in saturated fat and family history (NHS Essex ICB), plus ethnicity, sex and menopause (BHF). Inactivity, overweight, smoking and alcohol as causes were not stated in any returned text.
claims.newSentence: Causes and risk factors listed include eating a lot of food high in saturated fat and a family history of high cholesterol.

claims.evidence: BHF lists ethnicity, biological sex (males higher risk from a younger age) and menopause, and family history. 'Over 50' and the specific South Asian / sub-Saharan African groups were not in returned text.
claims.newSentence: It can also run in families, and the British Heart Foundation lists ethnicity, being male and having been through the menopause among the factors that raise risk.

claims.evidence: NHS: cut down on fatty food, especially food containing saturated fat.

NHS favours oily fish, olive or rapeseed oil, wholegrains, nuts and seeds; foods to limit named: meat pies, butter, cakes, coconut or palm oil. Cream, hard cheese and biscuits were not in returned text.
claims.newSentence: The NHS suggests unsaturated fats instead, such as oily fish, nuts, seeds and olive or rapeseed oil, and lists meat pies, butter, cakes and coconut or palm oil among foods to limit.

claims.evidence: BHF: oats and barley (soluble fibre) and beans, peas and lentils are sources of soluble fibre that help lower cholesterol.

HEART UK/Leeds trust leaflet: plant sterols and stanols in fortified foods (spreads) reduce cholesterol absorption. 'Yoghurt drinks' and 'not suitable for everyone' were not confirmed in returned text.
claims.newSentence: Plant sterols and stanols, added to some foods such as spreads, can also help lower cholesterol.

claims.evidence: The cited local 111 Wales/trust leaflet was not shown to say this. A national source does: BHF says dietary cholesterol has a minimal impact on blood cholesterol and cutting saturated fat matters more.
claims.newSentence: The British Heart Foundation says cholesterol in food has a minimal impact on blood cholesterol levels, and that cutting down on saturated fat matters more.

claims.evidence: NHS: you might need medicine if your cholesterol has not gone down after changing diet and lifestyle, or if at high risk of heart attack or stroke (medicines page).
NHS: statins are the most common medicine; you usually need to take them for life.
'Lipid profile' not found in returned text; the test is a blood test (NHS Health Check includes a cholesterol test).

NHS Health Check page: free check for adults in England aged 40 to 74 without existing conditions such as heart disease, diabetes or previous stroke; NHS Essex ICB says offered if aged 40 to 74 with no existing cardiovascular disease.
Returned summary (HEART UK/NHS-linked pages): a GP may suggest a test with high blood pressure, diabetes, overweight, smoking or family history of heart disease.
Returned text says targets depend on age and conditions such as diabetes or cardiovascular disease. 'Laboratory report' as setting targets was not stated.
claims.newSentence: Targets depend on factors such as age and other health conditions, so a clinician advises what applies to each person.

notes: c16 and c15 worded to national sources; the NHS main high-cholesterol page text came back partly garbled, so causes (c10) were limited to what other returned pages stated.
